transcript.content: Hi, welcome in — I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Well… things at work have gotten strange. Since I got this county safety award, some people have been messing with my inspection reports, or making it look that way, and asking these budget questions like they’re trying to pin something on me. My supervisor says it’s just normal review, but… I don’t think that’s all it is. It feels coordinated.
How long has this feeling that people are coordinating against you at work been going on—days, weeks, or longer?
Longer. About a year, I guess… since I got recognized for that county safety initiative. That’s when it started feeling like this.
Over this past year, have you had any stretches of time where your mood felt unusually high, energetic, or irritable, different from your normal self?
I don’t know… not really. I mean, I get irritated with what’s been going on, but I wouldn’t say I’ve had some big change like that.
Have you noticed anything unusual with your senses lately, like hearing voices or sounds that others don't seem to hear, or seeing things that aren't there?
No… I don’t think so. I mean, I haven’t been hearing voices or seeing things, if that’s what you mean.
Aside from these concerns about your coworkers, has your ability to function—like keeping up with your job duties, your relationships, or daily routines—changed at all over this past year?

I still do what I’m supposed to do. I’m on time, I get my inspections done, take care of myself… I still go to church.

It’s mostly when people start bringing up those reports, or asking about my spending, that things get… difficult.
Aside from what’s happening at work, do you have similar suspicions or beliefs about people—like neighbors, family, or strangers—trying to harm or interfere with you in other parts of your life?

No… not really. It’s mainly work.

After that county safety award, some people started acting different. My reports get picked apart, and then there are these pointed questions about budgets, like they’re trying to make me look crooked. My supervisor says it’s just normal review, but… I can tell it’s coordinated.
Do you drink alcohol, use any recreational drugs, or take medications that might affect your thinking or mood?
No… nothing like that, really. I mean, I’m not on anything that would mess with my head.
Have others told you that your speech or behavior seems disorganized, confused, or hard to follow at times?
Not that I know of. I mean… people don’t always like what I’m saying, but I don’t think I’m hard to follow.

When you think about these coworkers coordinating against you, do you feel completely certain that's what's happening, or is there any part of you that wonders if you might be misreading the situation?

I mean… I’m pretty sure. I don’t think I’m imagining it.

Ever since that safety award, the way they go over my reports and those budget questions… it feels too pointed to be random. My supervisor calls it normal review, but I can tell there’s something coordinated there.

When you think about how they're coordinating against you, do you believe they're using any unusual or extraordinary methods—like special technology, hacking, or something otherwise impossible—or is it more that they're using normal means, like meetings and emails, in a way that just seems overly focused on you?

No, not like… special technology or anything impossible. It’s more normal stuff. Meetings, emails, the way they review my inspection reports, the budget questions. Since that safety award, it just feels aimed at me, like they’re trying to make me look crooked.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with a single, well-systematized, non-bizarre persecutory delusion (coworkers coordinating to make him look dishonest via normal means—report reviews, budget questions) persisting for about one year. There are no hallucinations, no disorganized speech, no negative symptoms, and no mood episode (manic or depressive) accompanying the delusional belief. Functioning is largely preserved (work performance, self-care, church attendance intact), with impairment limited to distress around the delusional theme. The chronicity (>1 month, in fact ~1 year), absence of hallucinations/disorganization, and non-bizarre content using plausible mechanisms (meetings, emails, report review) rather than impossible means (technology, hacking) are classic for Delusional Disorder rather than Schizophrenia (which requires broader symptom criteria including disorganization or negative symptoms) or a mood disorder with psychotic features (no manic/depressive episode identified). No substance use or medical explanation identified.
